title: Walking between sittings
hookLine: slow walking meditation between periods of zazen

lines: A SLOW LINE AROUND THE HALL.
cards: The bell rings, and a period of zazen ends. Nobody heads for the door. Everyone stands, turns, and walks in a slow line around the hall.
One foot. Then, much later it seems, the other. Hands held together in front of the chest, eyes lowered.
Someone glancing through the window might think the whole room has slowed to half speed. In a way, it has. Knees that ached get to stretch, and the sitting goes on, upright and moving.

teach.b: First, sitting carried into motion. Kinhin comes between periods of zazen. The body gets a rest from crossed legs, but the attention doesn't take a break.
Second, the form. The hands are held in a particular way, often one hand closed loosely and the other wrapped over it, resting at the chest.

teach.h: HANDS AT THE CHEST, HALF A STEP.
teach.b: In many Soto halls, each breath carries the walker forward about half the length of a foot: step on the out-breath, pause, step again.

teach.h: SLOW IN ONE HALL, BRISK IN ANOTHER.
teach.b: Slow enough that walking stops being travel and becomes something you can feel: heel, sole, toes, weight shifting. Third, the schools differ.
In some Rinzai halls kinhin is brisk, almost a quick march, and it can wake a sleepy body in a hurry. Soto halls often keep it very slow. Neither is a mistake.
Both are the hall moving together, in one line, at one pace, nobody passing anybody.
Fourth, attention learns to stand up. The walk from the cushion to the door is the first step of the walk home.
Kinhin is the hinge. The point isn't to move strangely forever. It's to discover that attention can stand up with you, step out the door, and come along to the bus stop.
And when the bell ends kinhin, everyone goes straight back to the cushion, the same attention sitting down again.

how: In Zen halls, kinhin follows each period of zazen: practitioners walk in a line around the room with hands held at the chest, slowly in many Soto communities and more briskly in some Rinzai ones, until a bell calls them back to sit.

o: a quick stretch break once the meditation is over
slow walking meditation between periods of Zen sitting
a pilgrimage on foot to visit a well-known Zen temple

p: half a step on the out-breath
slow kinhin in many Soto halls

s: kinhin is a break from practice
the legs rest, but the attention doesn't: it's sitting carried into motion.
every Zen hall walks kinhin at the same slow pace
many Soto halls go very slowly; some Rinzai halls walk briskly.
the hall moves together, in one line, at one pace.

games.q: the bell ends a long sitting. your knees ache and you're ready to stretch. what does the hall do next?
o: everyone stands and walks slowly together in a line.
games.why: kinhin: the legs get to move, and the practice keeps going upright, until the bell calls the hall back to sit.

practice: If you have room, stand and rest your hands loosely together at your chest; breathe out and move one foot forward about half its length, feel the weight arrive, then breathe in and pause.
If standing isn't easy, do it seated: lift and place one foot, then the other, with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Kinhin. Walking meditation between periods of zazen: slow in many halls, brisk in some, always the same attention, carried on foot. Today's word.

orig.note: Japanese: kinhin, walking meditation in the Zen hall.

carryVoice: Your line: walking zen. The same attention as sitting, carried on foot. Same time tomorrow.

sources.work: Zen communal practice, Rinzai and Soto
